prompt: `aws configure set region us-east-1 --profile lab` wrote the region into which file?
hint: One file is for secrets only.

choices.text: `~/.aws/config`, under `[profile lab]`
choices.why: Right. Everything that is not a key goes there: region, output, role, process.

choices.text: `~/.aws/credentials`, beside the profile's keys
choices.why: That file holds keys and nothing else, which is what lets the other one be shared.

choices.text: `~/aws/env.sh`, which every terminal reads
choices.why: `env.sh` is this course's own file and the command line never writes to it.

choices.text: Neither: `configure set` changes only the current terminal
choices.why: `cat ~/.aws/config` showed the line afterwards. A variable would be the terminal-only kind.

prompt: How is the profile `lab` written as a section header in each of the two files?
hint: The default profile is the only one written the same in both.

choices.text: `[lab]` in both files
choices.why: That works for `credentials` only. In `config`, a bare name is how `[default]` and nothing else is written.

choices.text: `[profile lab]` in both files
choices.why: The `profile` prefix belongs to `config`; `credentials` uses the plain name.

choices.text: `[profile lab]` in `config` and `[lab]` in `credentials`
choices.why: Right. The transcript's two `cat` commands showed exactly that.

choices.text: `[sso-session lab]` in `config` and `[lab]` in `credentials`
choices.why: `sso-session` is a section for a sign-in, shared by profiles; it is not a profile.

prompt: The profile `lab` says `region = us-east-1`, and `env.sh` exports `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=sa-east-1`. Which region does `aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --profile lab` ask?
hint: Which layer is nearer?

choices.text: `sa-east-1`, because the variable beats the file
choices.why: Right. The first answer was `sa-east-1a`; only with `env -u AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` did the profile's region come through.

choices.text: `us-east-1`, because `--profile` takes precedence over the environment for every setting
choices.why: `--profile` removes the environment's keys, not its region. The exception is about credentials only.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: A command goes to one region. The settings decide which; they are not combined.

choices.text: Neither: the command line refuses when two regions are set
choices.why: Conflicts are the normal case, and the order of the layers settles them without a word.

prompt: Order the places a region can come from, from the one that wins to the one used last.
hint: Two variables, and one beats the other.
trap: `AWS_REGION` beats `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` when both are set, and both beat the file.

prompt: `aws configure ___ region --profile lab` printed `us-east-1`.
hint: The reading half of `set`.

prompt: The shop wants every developer's profiles to be the same. Why does splitting `config` from `credentials` make that safe to arrange?
hint: What can be copied around, and what must not be?

choices.text: Because `config` is encrypted and `credentials` is not
choices.why: Both are plain text. The safety comes from what each one holds.

choices.text: Because the command line ignores `credentials` once `config` exists
choices.why: Both are read; the transcript's `--profile lab` took its keys from `credentials` with `config` present.

choices.text: Because profiles in `config` cannot name an account
choices.why: They can: `role_arn` and `sso_account_id` both name one.

choices.text: `config` holds no secrets; the keys stay behind
choices.why: Right. A shared `config` with roles and `sso_session` profiles needs no `credentials` file at all.

prompt: `AWS_PROFILE=lab aws configure list` shows the profile `lab` but `env` in the `TYPE` column for the keys. Why?
hint: Lesson 10's chain, and what a variable does to it.

choices.text: The `env` provider comes first, and `AWS_PROFILE` leaves it in the chain
choices.why: Right. The test keys `env.sh` exported answered before the profile's file was looked at.

choices.text: Because the profile `lab` has no keys of its own
choices.why: It has them; `--profile lab` read them from `shared-credentials-file` a moment later.

choices.text: Because `AWS_PROFILE` is only read by the SDKs, not the command line
choices.why: The command line read it: the `profile` row says `lab`, from `AWS_PROFILE`.

choices.text: Because `configure list` always reports the environment, whatever is used
choices.why: With `--profile` it reported `shared-credentials-file`. It reports what would be used.

prompt: In the profile `staging`, what does `source_profile = lab` name?
hint: Assuming a role needs credentials of its own.

choices.text: The account the role lives in
choices.why: The account is inside `role_arn`. `source_profile` is about who asks.

choices.text: A profile to fall back on if the role cannot be assumed
choices.why: There is no fallback: if `AssumeRole` fails, the command fails.

choices.text: The profile whose credentials call `sts:AssumeRole`
choices.why: Right. `lab`'s keys signed the `AssumeRole`, and the role's temporary credentials signed the command.

choices.text: The profile whose region and output are inherited
choices.why: Settings are not inherited: `staging` printed a table because it said `output = table` itself.

prompt: `credential_process = sh ~/aws/lab-creds.sh` fails with `cannot open ~/aws/lab-creds.sh`, although the file is there. Why?
hint: Who expands `~`?

choices.text: Because the script is not executable
choices.why: It is run as an argument to `sh`, which needs no execute bit. The path itself is the problem.

choices.text: Because `credential_process` only accepts Python programs
choices.why: Any program that prints the JSON will do; the working version runs the same `sh` script.

choices.text: Because the environment's keys stopped the process from starting
choices.why: With `--profile` those keys are out of the chain, and the process did start: `sh` printed the error.

choices.text: The command is not run by a shell, so `~` reaches `sh` unexpanded
choices.why: Right. `sh -c "sh ~/aws/lab-creds.sh"` hands the line to a shell, which does expand it.

prompt: Match each setting of a role profile to what it does.
hint: Two came up in the transcript, two in the paragraph after it.

pairs.right: use the environment or metadata instead

right_distractors: the region the role lives in

prompt: What happens if you delete the `.json` files in `~/.aws/cli/cache/`?
hint: They are a copy of something the command line can get again.

choices.text: The profile `staging` stops working until it is written again
choices.why: The profile lives in `~/.aws/config`. The cache only saves a call.

choices.text: Nothing breaks: the next command assumes the role again
choices.why: Right. They hold the role's temporary credentials until they expire, to avoid an `AssumeRole` per command.

choices.text: The keys of `lab` are lost
choices.why: Those are in `~/.aws/credentials`, which the cache never touches.

choices.text: Every session opened with the role is revoked in the account
choices.why: Deleting a local file changes nothing in AWS; the credentials simply stop being kept here.

prompt: Whose credentials does the command line in AWS CloudShell use?
hint: There is nothing to configure.

choices.text: A key created for CloudShell when it is first opened
choices.why: No key is created. CloudShell borrows the session of whoever opened it.

choices.text: The account root user's
choices.why: Only somebody signed in as root would get root. Everybody else gets their own identity.

choices.text: Whatever `~/.aws/credentials` holds on your laptop
choices.why: CloudShell runs on AWS's side and never sees your laptop's files.

choices.text: Those of the console session that opened it
choices.why: Right. They end when that session does, and the person acts as themselves.

prompt: Which of these can a profile use to get its credentials? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section ends with a list of four.

choices.text: Keys in `~/.aws/credentials`
choices.why: Right. The profile `lab`, read as `shared-credentials-file`.

choices.text: A role assumed with another profile's credentials
choices.why: Right. `role_arn` and `source_profile`, as `staging` does.

choices.text: A program named in `credential_process`
choices.why: Right. Its JSON output is the credentials, reported as `custom-process`.

choices.text: A sign-in through Identity Center, with `sso_session`
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11's profile, filled by `aws sso login`.

choices.text: A web page whose address is in the profile
choices.why: No setting fetches credentials from a page. The access portal is opened by a person, not by a profile.

prompt: A `--query` filter on `aws iam list-policies --scope AWS` keeps the sixteen policies whose names start with `AmazonS3`. How much did IAM send?
hint: Where is `--query` evaluated?

choices.text: Only the sixteen policies the filter matched
choices.why: That is what a server-side `--filters` would do. `--query` runs after the answer arrives.

choices.text: Only the names, since the query asked for nothing else
choices.why: The API returns whole policy records; the projection to names happens locally.

choices.text: Every policy; the filter ran locally
choices.why: Right. JMESPath is evaluated by the command line on the full answer, so the listing costs the same.

choices.text: One page of 100 policies
choices.why: The command line followed every marker, as the 16 requests in `--debug` showed.

prompt: A shell script splits the command line's answer with `cut`. Which `--output` suits it?
hint: Values separated by tabs.

choices.text: `table`, since its columns line up
choices.why: The borders and padding are for eyes; `cut` would get them as part of every value.

choices.text: `text`
choices.why: Right. One value per tab-separated column, ideally after a `--query` that fixes the order.

choices.text: `yaml`, which is the easiest to read
choices.why: Easy for people, awkward for `cut`: keys and values share each line.

choices.text: `json`, piped through `cut -d:`
choices.why: JSON is for a JSON parser such as `jq`; splitting it on colons breaks on the first nested value.

prompt: `aws ec2 run-instances … --dry-run` prints an error and exits with 254. What does that say?
hint: Read the error code, not the exit code.

choices.text: That the image does not exist in `sa-east-1`
choices.why: A missing image is a different error. This one says the request would have succeeded.

choices.text: That the instance was started and then stopped
choices.why: Nothing was started: `describe-instances` counted 0 reservations afterwards.

choices.text: `DryRunOperation`: allowed, and nothing made
choices.why: Right. A refused dry run is `UnauthorizedOperation` instead, so a script tells them apart by the code.

choices.text: That `--dry-run` is not supported by `run-instances`
choices.why: It is one of the calls EC2 accepts it on; the error is how a successful dry run answers.

prompt: moto holds 1544 AWS-managed policies, and `ListPolicies` returns 100 per call. How many requests does the command line send to list them all?
hint: Round up.

prompt: What is the difference between `--page-size 500` and `--max-items 500` on a listing of 1544 policies?
hint: One changes the requests, the other the answer.

choices.text: `--page-size` asks for bigger pages and prints all 1544; `--max-items` prints 500 and a token
choices.why: Right. The token lets `--starting-token` carry on from where `--max-items` stopped.

choices.text: None: both return 500 policies
choices.why: `--page-size 500` still returned all 1544, in 4 requests instead of 16.

choices.text: `--page-size` filters on the server; `--max-items` filters locally
choices.why: Neither filters. One sets how much each request asks for, the other where the printed answer stops.

choices.text: `--max-items` is the old name of `--page-size`
choices.why: Both exist side by side and do different things, as the two transcripts showed.

prompt: In a JMESPath expression, a literal string such as `AmazonS3` is written between ___, each escaped with a backslash inside the shell's double quotes.
hint: The same character the shell uses for command substitution.

prompt: With `env.sh` read, `ana` wants every command in one terminal to run as the profile `staging` without typing `--profile`. What does she type?
hint: A variable alone loses to the environment's keys.

choices.text: `export AWS_PROFILE=staging`
choices.why: The test keys `env.sh` exported would still answer first, as `AWS_PROFILE=lab` showed.

choices.text: `unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and then `export AWS_PROFILE=staging`
choices.why: Right. With the keys gone, the profile is the first thing the chain finds, and the endpoint stays pointed at moto.

choices.text: `aws configure set default.profile staging`
choices.why: There is no such setting, and the environment's keys would win over any file anyway.

choices.text: Edit `env.sh` to remove the keys for every lesson
choices.why: It would work here and break every other lesson, which relies on those keys.

prompt: A teammate's script runs `aws ec2 describe-vpcs --output table` and picks the VPC id out with `awk`. It breaks when a VPC gets a tag. What is the sturdier way?
hint: Ask for exactly the field, in a format meant for programs.

choices.text: Keep the table and widen the `awk` pattern
choices.why: The table's layout follows the data, so the next change breaks the wider pattern too.

choices.text: Switch to `--output yaml` and search for `VpcId:`
choices.why: Better than a table, and still a search through text that a nested field can confuse.

choices.text: `--query "Vpcs[].VpcId" --output text`
choices.why: Right. The query fixes the field and the order, and `text` hands the shell plain values.

choices.text: Add `--no-paginate` so the table has fewer rows
choices.why: Fewer pages is not fewer columns, and it silently drops VPCs past the first page.

prompt: A laptop has no `env.sh`, `AWS_PROFILE=staging` exported, and the profile `staging` with `role_arn` and `source_profile = lab`. Which credentials sign `aws s3 ls`?
hint: No keys in the environment this time.

choices.text: `lab`'s keys, since they are the only long-term ones
choices.why: They sign the `AssumeRole`. The command itself is signed with what that returns.

choices.text: The instance metadata service's, at the bottom of the chain
choices.why: The chain stops at the first answer, and the profile answers long before the metadata provider.

choices.text: None: `AWS_PROFILE` is ignored without `--profile`
choices.why: It is ignored only for keys that the environment already supplies; here there are none.

choices.text: Temporary credentials for the role in `role_arn`, obtained with `lab`'s keys
choices.why: Right. With nothing in the environment, `AWS_PROFILE` decides, and the profile's role is assumed and cached.
